title: per-token-latency-field-lab-competitive-annotated
content:
Purpose: capture field-lab experiments + annotated competitive notes to support conservative go-to-market claims about latency-to-cost (ms -> $) and why Redwood is meaningfully faster/cheaper for production inference workloads. This is a working doc — experimental logs, customer scripts, and an evidence hierarchy are intentionally rough.

TL;DR (recommended conservative claims we can support today):
- For 2–4k token end-to-end chat interactions on dedicated-grade hardware, Redwood p50 latency is typically 30–60ms per token lower than LargeCloud-style managed endpoints when using continuous batching + KV-prefix caching (measured on H100 pools with rw-70b-q4 baseline).
- With workload-aware batching + prefix caching, per-token serving cost (GPU amortized + infra) drops ~25–40% versus naive per-request serving (no KV cache, small batch sizes) on identical hardware and model families.
- For conversational session workloads where >50% of tokens are repeated context, Redwood’s automatic KV caching reduces total token compute by 30–60%, translating to a 20–45% effective dollar-per-session saving depending on sequence lengths and cache locality.

How to read these numbers: conservative margins and exacts \u2014 these are field-lab medians across 8 customer-like workloads (search+chat, support assistant, summarization bursty load). We intentionally avoid absolute single-number claims (e.g., "Redwood is X% cheaper than CompetitorY") without customer-specific lab reproduction. Instead: "typical savings range" + reproducible method.

Experiment summary (annotated):
- Workloads tested:
  - Support-chat (avg prompt 600 tokens, response 400 tokens, session reuse 65%)
  - Document-summarization (single-shot 3k tokens output, low cache reuse)
  - Search-re-ranking (short outputs 50-150 tokens, high QPS burstiness)
- Models & variants:
  - rw-70b (float32 baseline), rw-70b-q4 (quantized), rw-13b-q4-lite (cheap variant)
  - open-70b-q4 (public baseline used for cross-vendor parity testing)
- Hardware: H100 80GB dedicated pools vs A100 40GB baselines
- Serving configs compared: continuous-batching + prefix-KV vs fixed-microbatch (N=8, delay 10ms) vs single-request
- Measurement window: 30-minute steady runs + controlled microburst tests (10k requests at 500rps sustained for 5s)

Representative numbers (field medians):
- Support-chat (rw-70b-q4 on H100):
  - Redwood continuous-batching + KV: p50 token latency 42ms, p95 token latency 120ms, mean cost per token (infra+gpu amortized) = $0.00021
  - Fixed microbatch (delay=10ms): p50 63ms, p95 240ms, cost per token = $0.00028
  - Naive single-request: p50 95ms, p95 480ms, cost per token = $0.00036
- Summarization (long output, low cache): continuous-batching advantage narrows but still reduces mean cost ~18% vs single-request because of batching efficiencies.

Annotated competitive notes (high level, do not be absolutist):
- LargeCloud-style managed endpoints: typically favor fixed microbatching across multi-tenant nodes which reduces tail under steady high throughput but is conservative for bursty chat; we see higher p95 in burst scenarios due to queueing and lack of aggressive prefix caching.
- OtherLLMAPI: sometimes advertises low p50 on short sequences but charges per-request overheads and limited routing controls; real customer workloads with mixed seq lengths produce higher unit costs.
- Key Redwood differentiator (evidence-backed): ability to route in-sessional traffic to cache-friendly paths + continuous batching that opportunistically fuses micro-opportunities without introducing fixed queuing delays. Evidence: latency traces + replayed traffic show ~1.6x higher throughput for same latency envelope versus fixed-delay microbatching. See linked PR for trace visualizations.

Proof mapping (claim -> what to show in sales/ops materials):
- Claim: "Redwood reduces per-session cost by up to 40% for chat-heavy workloads."
  - Evidence: experiment logs (JIRA-9876), per-session token breakdown CSV (attached in bench PR), customer replay that shows cache hit rate and compute reduction.
- Claim: "Lower p95 on microbursts keeps user-facing latency below slas."
  - Evidence: microburst trace set (github PR), comparison heatmaps vs LargeCloud.

Sample customer briefing script (short):
- Sales opener: "We audited a few production workloads similar to yours. By combining persistent KV caching and Redwoods continuous batching, we reduced p50 token latency and cut per-session GPU costs by ~25-40% in our lab replays — which means faster responses for your users and a predictable per-month bill. Can we run a 48-hour replay of a small slice of your traffic?"
- Demo play: play two recorded sessions side-by-side (Redwood vs fixed-microbatch) highlighting end-to-end time-to-first-token and total tokens computed.

Conservative messaging rules (to stick to legal/comms constraints):
- Always quote ranges and the workload used to produce the numbers.
- Avoid direct named competitor percentage claims in customer-facing slide decks (internal notes can be frank but customer claims must be framed as "in our lab replays vs common managed endpoints").
- Include resource footnote: hardware class, model family, and cache assumptions (e.g., "H100-class, rw-70b-q4, 60% session-level cache locality").

Open questions + experiments to run next (prioritized):
1) Heavy-multitenant stress: run 24h of mixed-tenancy tests to quantify isolation tail effects across reserved pools (target: reproduce p95 shift >10%?).
2) Routing fallbacks: measure cost/latency delta when falling back from rw-70b-q4 to rw-13b-q4-lite for low-priority traffic at 10k QPS.
3) Edge-region delta: reproduce tests in eu-west and ap-southeast to quantify network overhead + routing latency.

Risk notes:
- Results are sensitive to model family and quantization: older quant kernels can show regressed latency (higher p95) despite lower token costs.
- Customer traffic with extremely high-context-drift (low cache reuse) will see smaller savings; do not promise >40% in those cases.

Appendix (quick reproducibility checklist):
- Repo: github.com/redwood-inference/rw-benchmarks (PR 42 has bench scripts used)
- Repro steps: replay traffic -> enable continuous batcher -> enable prefix-KV -> collect per-token latencies and GPU-side counters -> normalize costs using our GPU amortization table (contrib/GPU-costs.csv)
- Contact: Aisha Kumar (owner) for bench artifacts; Benji Park for trace visualizations.

Next actions for GTM:
- Convert key plots into 1-page "bench-to-dollar" slide (show p50/p95 + per-token $ bands) for AE battle cards.
- Draft conservative sales one-liner and 2 example customer scripts for pilot ask.
- Schedule 2 lab reproductions (EU and APAC) and capture results into Confluence-1234.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc lean; move final reproducible tables into bench PR and lock claim language in the sales artifact review thread.
